raw_response:
*Speaking in first person as the farmer:*

Aiya, this land — I've been working it forty years. Two mu, that's all. My old man and me do most of it. Three of my boys went to Handan and Beijing for work long ago, they send money home but only come back at holidays. The daughter-in-law helps when she can, the grandkids are still small.

For wheat, I plant after National Day, around the start of the tenth month when the ground is ready. Seed from the shop, sometimes I keep some from last year if it looked good — scatter it thick, about fifteen, sixteen jin per mu, because the cold kills some. Before planting I spread one bag of the 15-15-15 compound per mu — that's what everyone around here does. Then in spring at jointing, when the wheat stands up tall, I put down half a bag of urea per mu and water it in. I water maybe three times — once before the cold, once with the urea, once when the grain is filling if it's dry. The pump costs money but you can't let the wheat dry out then.

Wheat comes off early sixth month. Last year was dry, I had to water extra. Got maybe six, seven hundred jin per mu — not bad, some years worse.

Then maize right after, no time. The village machine-man comes through, rototills and plants same day — sixty yuan a mu, everyone uses him. Hybrid seed from the shop, whatever they have. Less fertilizer on maize than on wheat, maize isn't so hungry — one bag of compound, and if the leaves look pale I sprinkle some urea when it's knee-high. If no rain at tasseling I water once. For the borer I put the granules in the whorl, cheap enough.

Herbicide for the wheat once in spring — I'm too old to hoe two mu by myself. For maize I pull weeds when I walk the field.

All together for the year maybe a thousand, twelve hundred yuan for the two mu. The grain mostly feeds us and the chickens, sell some maize if the price is okay. Can't spend more than we have.
